questions.question: Which operator is used with cin to accept input?
questions.explanation: The extraction operator >> transfers data from an input stream to a variable.

questions.question: Which OOP feature binds data and related functions into one unit?
questions.answer: C. Encapsulation
questions.explanation: A class encapsulates state and operations in one logical unit.

questions.question: Memory obtained using new should normally be released using:
questions.answer: D. delete

questions.question: State any three differences between C and C++.
questions.answer: C is primarily procedural; C++ supports procedural and object-oriented programming. C has no classes or function overloading; C++ supports both. C commonly uses malloc/free; C++ provides new/delete and constructors/destructors.

questions.question: Define abstraction and encapsulation with one example of each.
questions.answer: Abstraction presents essential behaviour while hiding internal detail, such as calling withdraw() without knowing banking logic. Encapsulation bundles data and methods and controls access, such as a BankAccount class with private balance and public deposit().

questions.question: What is a constructor? List its main characteristics.
questions.answer: A constructor is a special member function invoked automatically when an object is created. It has the class name, no return type, may be overloaded and normally initialises object state.

questions.question: Differentiate a shallow copy from a deep copy.
questions.answer: A shallow copy duplicates member values, so pointer members may refer to the same resource. A deep copy allocates a separate resource and copies its contents, preventing accidental sharing and double deletion.

questions.question: Differentiate aggregation and composition.
questions.answer: Both are has-a relationships. In aggregation the part can exist independently of the whole; in composition the whole owns the part and controls its lifetime. A Department–Teacher relation may aggregate; a House–Room relation commonly composes.

questions.question: Explain the effect of public, protected and private inheritance on public and protected base members.
questions.answer: Public inheritance preserves public as public and protected as protected. Protected inheritance makes both protected. Private inheritance makes both private. Private base members are never directly accessible in the derived class.

questions.question: What is function overloading? Give a valid example signature pair.
questions.answer: Function overloading defines several functions with the same name but different parameter lists, e.g. int area(int) and double area(double,double). Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.

questions.question: Why should a polymorphic base class usually have a virtual destructor?
questions.answer: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer must invoke both derived and base destructors. A virtual base destructor enables correct dynamic dispatch and prevents leaked derived resources.

questions.question: What problem do namespaces solve?
questions.answer: Namespaces group names and prevent collisions between identifiers from different libraries or modules. A name can be qualified, for example college::Student.

questions.question: What is template specialisation?
questions.answer: Template specialisation supplies a custom implementation for a particular type or set of template arguments when the general template is unsuitable or can be improved.

questions.question: Name the main file-stream classes and state their purposes.
questions.answer: ifstream reads files, ofstream writes files, and fstream supports both input and output.

questions.question: Explain try, throw and catch.
questions.answer: Code that may fail is placed in try. throw signals an exceptional condition and passes an exception object. A matching catch block receives and handles it.

questions.question: Explain the four major principles of object-oriented programming with suitable C++ examples.
questions.answer: Discuss abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Define each, show how class access control implements encapsulation, an interface exposes abstraction, a derived class reuses a base class, and virtual functions provide runtime polymorphism. Include a compact class hierarchy example.

questions.question: Explain default, parameterised and copy constructors, constructor overloading, and destructors.
questions.answer: Define each constructor type with syntax and invocation. Explain overloaded constructors and initialiser lists. Describe automatic destructor invocation, reverse destruction order and resource release. A complete Resource class example earns full credit.

questions.question: Explain all major types of inheritance with diagrams or class declarations. Also discuss ambiguity.
questions.answer: Cover single, multilevel, multiple, hierarchical and hybrid inheritance. Include access modes, constructor/destructor order, ambiguity caused by identical inherited names, explicit qualification and virtual inheritance for the diamond problem.

questions.question: Compare compile-time and runtime polymorphism in C++.
questions.answer: Compile-time polymorphism uses function/operator overloading and is resolved by the compiler. Runtime polymorphism uses overriding through virtual functions and base pointers/references, resolved by dynamic binding. Give code, benefits, limitations and a comparison table.

questions.question: Explain function templates and class templates with complete examples.
questions.answer: Describe generic programming, template parameters, instantiation and type substitution. Provide one generic maximum function and one Stack<T> class, then mention specialisation and compile-time type checking.

questions.question: Explain exception handling in C++, including multiple handlers, catch-all handlers, rethrowing and user-defined exceptions.
questions.answer: Describe normal control flow through try, throw and matching catch blocks. Explain handler order, catch(...), throw; for rethrowing, exception objects/classes, stack unwinding, and why exceptions should be caught by reference.
